cse-1997-a-43.approach: Equivalence relations on a set correspond one-to-one with its partitions, so count the partitions of a 4-element set (the Bell number $B_4$).
concepts: Stirling numbers of the second kind

steps.title: Relations ↔ partitions
steps.body: Every equivalence relation splits $\{1,2,3,4\}$ into equivalence classes (a partition), and every partition defines exactly one equivalence relation. So the answer is the number of partitions $B_4$.

steps.title: Count by number of blocks
steps.body:
Using $S(4,k)$ = partitions into $k$ non-empty blocks:

| $k$ | shape | $S(4,k)$ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $\{1234\}$ | 1 |
| 2 | $3+1$ or $2+2$ | $4+3=7$ |
| 3 | $2+1+1$ | $\binom42=6$ |
| 4 | $1+1+1+1$ | 1 |

For $k=2$: choosing the singleton gives $4$; splitting into two pairs gives $\binom42/2=3$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $B_4=15$ partitions, hence 15 equivalence relations.
16 is $2^4$, the number of subsets — not partitions.
24 is $4!$, the number of permutations.
4 counts only the possible numbers of blocks $k=1..4$.

pitfalls: Counting reflexive/symmetric relations instead of partitions.
For the $2+2$ split, forgetting to divide $\binom42$ by 2.

cse-1997-a-44.approach: A string avoids 100 exactly when no two 0s follow a 1. After the leading 0s, the string is built only from the blocks 1 and 10.

steps.title: Structure of valid strings
steps.body: Before the first 1, any number of 0s is harmless: $0^*$. After the first 1, two consecutive 0s would form $100$ (with the last 1 before them). So every 0 after that point comes alone, right after a 1. The rest of the string is therefore a sequence of the blocks $1$ and $10$: $(1+10)^*$.

steps.title: Match with options
steps.body: That is $0^*(10+1)^*$ = option D. It allows strings like $1010$, $110$ and a trailing $10$, but no block sequence can produce $00$ after a 1.

steps.title: Reject the others
steps.body:
- A: $(1^*0)(1^*0)$ with $1^*=1$ then $1^*=\varepsilon$ gives $10\cdot0 = 100$, so A contains a forbidden string.
- B: $0^*1010^*$ contains $10100$, which has $100$, and misses $1$.
- C: $0^*1^*01^*$ needs exactly one 0 after the 1s, so it misses $\varepsilon$ and $1$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Generates $100$ (as $(10)(0)$), so it does not avoid the substring.
Generates $10100$, which contains $100$; also misses valid strings such as $1$.
Every string has a 0 right after the block of 1s; misses $\varepsilon$, $1$ and $1010$.
After the leading 0s, only the blocks $1$ and $10$, so $00$ never follows a 1.

pitfalls: Checking only that an option avoids $100$ — it must also generate every valid string.
cse-1997-a-44.verification: Listed all strings of length ≤ 3 without 100 (all except 100 itself): each is $0^*$ followed by blocks 1/10, e.g. 010 = 0·10, 110 = 1·10.

cse-1997-a-45.approach: Check each problem against standard results: bounded simulation and emptiness of FA/CFG are decidable; equivalence of Turing machines is undecidable (Rice's theorem).

steps.title: Decidable ones
steps.body:
- A: simulate $M$ on $s$ for at most $k$ steps — always halts.
- C: FSM emptiness — check whether a final state is reachable from the start state.
- D: CFG emptiness — mark generating variables iteratively and check whether $S$ is generating.

steps.title: Undecidable one
steps.body: B: $\{\langle M_1,M_2\rangle : L(M_1)=L(M_2)\}$ is undecidable. Even "$L(M)=\emptyset$" is undecidable (Rice's theorem), and emptiness reduces to equivalence with a machine that rejects everything.

optionAnalysis.reason: Bounded by $k$ steps, so direct simulation decides it.
TM equivalence is undecidable (not even semi-decidable).
Reachability of a final state in a finite graph — decidable.
The generating-symbol algorithm decides CFG emptiness.

pitfalls: Confusing A with the halting problem — the step bound $k$ makes it decidable.
cse-1997-a-45.verification: Reduction $E_{TM}\le EQ_{TM}$: compare $M$ with a machine that rejects every input.

cse-1997-a-46.approach: A DPDA must know where the middle of the string is. The centre marker $c$ gives exactly that in option A; the other languages lack it or are not context-free.

steps.title: Option A is deterministic
steps.body: Push each $a/b$ until $c$ is read; after $c$ pop and match each symbol; accept when the stack is back to the bottom marker at the end of input. Every move is forced, so a DPDA accepts $\{wcw^R\}$.

steps.title: Why the rest fail
steps.body:
- B ($ww^R$) and D (all palindromes) need a guess of the middle: they are CFLs that no DPDA accepts.
- C ($a^nb^nc^n$) is not even context-free (pumping lemma).

optionAnalysis.reason: The marker $c$ tells the machine when to switch from pushing to popping.
Even-length palindromes — the middle must be guessed; not a DCFL.
Not context-free at all.
Palindromes over $\{a,b,c\}$ — here $c$ is an ordinary symbol, not a marker, so the middle must still be guessed.

pitfalls: In D the symbol $c$ can appear anywhere, so it does not act as a centre marker.
cse-1997-a-46.verification: Traced the DPDA for A on $abcba$: push a, b; read c; pop b, a — accepts.

cse-1997-a-47.approach: Worst case: each process holds one unit less than it needs. If one more unit exists, some process can finish. So the minimum is $n(k-1)+1$.

steps.title: Deadlock with 3 units
steps.body: With 3 units, each of the 3 processes can hold 1 unit and wait for its second — circular wait, deadlock.

steps.title: Add one unit
steps.body: $$n(k-1)+1 = 3(2-1)+1 = 4$$ With 4 units, even when each process holds 1, one unit is free; some process gets its 2nd unit, finishes and releases both.

optionAnalysis.reason: Each process can hold 1 unit and wait forever — deadlock is possible.
Deadlock-free, but not the minimum.
$3\cdot1+1=4$ is the smallest deadlock-free count.
Enough for all at once, but more than needed.

pitfalls: Answering $n\cdot k=6$ (no waiting at all) instead of the minimum.
cse-1997-a-47.verification: With 3 units the state (1,1,1) is a deadlock; with 4 units every maximal holding state leaves a free unit.

cse-1997-a-48.approach: Look for the worst interleaving. $P_{10}$ performs V instead of P, so each pass of $P_{10}$ adds to mutex instead of taking it. It can let every other process in.

steps.title: Effect of $P_{10}$
steps.body: mutex starts at 1. $P_{10}$ executes `V(mutex)` (mutex $+1$), enters the CS without blocking, does `V(mutex)` again on exit ($+1$), and loops. Each round adds 2 to mutex.

steps.title: Build the worst case
steps.body: $P_1$ enters (mutex $1\to0$). $P_{10}$ enters with V (mutex $0\to1$), so $P_2$ can enter (mutex $1\to0$). $P_{10}$ leaves with V (mutex $0\to1$), so $P_3$ enters. $P_{10}$ loops and does V again, and so on. In this way $P_1,\dots,P_9$ all get inside, and $P_{10}$ itself can be inside too.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: Up to all $10$ processes can be in the critical section at once. That is not 1, 2 or 3, so the answer is "none of above".

optionAnalysis.reason: Only true if every process used P before entering.
Assumes $P_{10}$ lets in just one extra process; it can do V again and again.
Counts only one extra pass of $P_{10}$.
All 10 processes can be inside together.

pitfalls: Forgetting that $P_{10}$ loops forever, so it can do V many times.
cse-1997-a-48.verification: Tracked mutex through the sequence above: it never goes below 0 when a new process enters, so nobody blocks.

cse-1997-a-49.approach: Find the candidate key, then check for partial dependencies of non-prime attributes on part of the key.

steps.title: Key
steps.body: $a$ and $b$ never appear on a right side, so both are in every key. $\{a,b\}^+ = \{a,b,c,d\}$, so the only candidate key is $ab$. Prime: $a,b$; non-prime: $c,d$.

steps.title: Check 2NF
steps.body: $a\to c$: the non-prime attribute $c$ depends on a proper subset of the key. That is a partial dependency, so 2NF is violated (likewise $b\to d$).

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: All domains are atomic, so $R$ is in 1NF but not in 2NF.

optionAnalysis.reason: Atomic values give 1NF; $a\to c$ is a partial dependency.
Not in 2NF because of the partial dependencies.
3NF implies 2NF, which fails.
Option A describes it correctly.

pitfalls: Treating $a$ alone as a key — $a^+=\{a,c\}$ only.
cse-1997-a-49.verification: $a^+=\{a,c\}$, $b^+=\{b,d\}$, $(ab)^+$ = all attributes — so $ab$ is the only key.

cse-1997-a-50.approach: Referential integrity breaks only when a foreign-key value in S has no matching key in R. Ask which operation can create such a dangling reference.

steps.title: Operations on S (referencing)
steps.body:
- Insert into S: the new tuple's $d$ may not exist in R, so it **can** violate.
- Delete from S: removing a referencing tuple never leaves anything dangling.

steps.title: Operations on R (referenced)
steps.body:
- Insert into R: adds a new key, so no reference can break.
- Delete from R: tuples of S that refer to the deleted key become dangling, so it **can** violate.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Only (2) and (3) can cause a violation.

optionAnalysis.reason: (2) and (3) can violate it.
(1) and (4) can never violate it.
These are exactly the two safe operations.
Insert into the referencing table, delete from the referenced table.

pitfalls: Mixing up the referencing table (S) and the referenced table (R).
cse-1997-a-50.verification: For each operation, checked whether some S tuple can end up with a $d$ value missing from R.

cse-1997-a-51-a.approach: Decode the I/O write cycle to port FFH with one NAND gate: all 8 address bits, $IO/\overline{M}$, and an active-high write strobe (the NOT gate inverts $\overline{WR}$). The NAND output clocks the D flip-flop with $D_3$ on D, and the 8085 reset drives the clear.
cse-1997-a-51-a.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Port | FFH (I/O mapped, `OUT FFH`) |
| Data bit | $D_3$ |
| Parts | 1 NAND (10 inputs), 1 NOT, 1 D flip-flop |
| Clear | on power ON |

steps.title: Which signals identify the cycle
steps.body: For `OUT FFH` the 8085 puts the port address on $A_7$–$A_0$ (copied on $A_{15}$–$A_8$). During the I/O write machine cycle $IO/\overline{M}=1$ and $\overline{WR}=0$. So a write to port FFH means $A_7=\dots=A_0=1$, $IO/\overline{M}=1$ and $WR=1$.

steps.title: Decoder: NAND + NOT
steps.body:
NOT gate: $WR=\overline{\overline{WR}}$. NAND inputs (10): $A_0,\dots,A_7$, $IO/\overline{M}$, $WR$.

$$\text{CLK}=\overline{A_7A_6\cdots A_0\cdot IO/\overline{M}\cdot WR}$$

CLK is low only while the CPU writes to port FFH.

steps.title: Latch the data
steps.body: Connect $D_3$ to the D input and the NAND output to CLK. At the end of the write, $\overline{WR}$ rises, so CLK has a rising edge while $D_3$ is still valid. The flip-flop stores $D_3$, and Q is the 1-bit output port.

steps.title: Clear on power ON
steps.body: Connect the 8085 reset to the flip-flop's clear: RESET OUT (active high) to an active-high CLR, or $\overline{\text{RESET IN}}$ (the power-on RC signal, active low) to an active-low $\overline{\text{CLR}}$. Then Q = 0 after power ON.

answer.value: NAND inputs: $A_0$–$A_7$, $IO/\overline{M}$ and $WR$ (= NOT of $\overline{WR}$). The NAND output clocks the D flip-flop (rising edge at the end of the OUT write cycle). D input = $D_3$. The clear input comes from the 8085 reset (RESET OUT, or $\overline{\text{RESET IN}}$ to an active-low clear), so the flip-flop is cleared at power ON.

pitfalls: Leaving out $IO/\overline{M}$ — a memory write to an address xxFFH would then also clock the port.
Clocking on the falling edge of $\overline{WR}$ — the data is surely stable only at the rising edge.
cse-1997-a-51-a.verification: Counted NAND inputs: 8 address + $IO/\overline{M}$ + $WR$ = 10, matching the fan-in. The NOT gate is used once, for $\overline{WR}$.

cse-1997-a-51-b.approach: Write D3 with `OUT`, flip all bits of A with `CMA`, and jump back. `OUT` (3 machine cycles) + `CMA` (1) + `JMP` (3) = 7 bus cycles between two writes, so ON and OFF each last 7 bus cycles.

steps.title: Program
steps.body:
```
      MVI A, 00H   ; D3 = 0 (any start value)
LOOP: OUT FFH      ; latch D3 into the flip-flop
      CMA          ; complement A, so D3 toggles
      JMP LOOP
```

steps.title: Bus (machine) cycles per loop
steps.body:
| Instruction | Machine cycles |
|---|---|
| `OUT FFH` | opcode fetch, memory read (port no.), I/O write = 3 |
| `CMA` | opcode fetch = 1 |
| `JMP LOOP` | opcode fetch, 2 memory reads = 3 |
| **Total** | $3+1+3=7$ |

steps.title: Time between output changes
steps.body: The output changes only in the I/O write cycle of `OUT`. From one I/O write to the next: CMA (1) + JMP (3) + OUT fetch and read (2) + the new I/O write (1) $= 7$ bus cycles. So each ON and each OFF level lasts 7 bus cycles.

answer.value: `MVI A,00H` ; `LOOP: OUT FFH` ; `CMA` ; `JMP LOOP` — 3 + 1 + 3 = 7 bus cycles per half-period.

pitfalls: Counting T-states instead of bus (machine) cycles.
Putting `MVI` inside the loop — it adds 2 cycles and stops the toggling.
cse-1997-a-51-b.verification: Cycles from write to write: CMA 1, JMP 3, OUT fetch 1, OUT read 1, write 1 → 7.

cse-1997-a-52.approach: Recursive pairwise swap: for nodes $p$ (1st) and $q$ (2nd), $q$ becomes the head, $q$ points to $p$, and $p$ points to the swapped rest of the list starting at $t=q\uparrow.next$.

steps.title: Base cases (lines 4–5)
steps.body: Empty list: return `p` (nil). One node: nothing to swap, so the line 5 box is **`p`**.

steps.title: Name the pieces (lines 7, 9)
steps.body: `q := p↑.next` is the 2nd node; `t := q↑.next` is the rest of the list, starting at node 3.

scene.caption: p = a1, q = a2, t = a3

steps.title: New head (line 8)
steps.body: After the swap $a_2$ comes first, so line 8 is **`change := q`**. In Pascal the function result may be assigned before the end.

steps.title: Relink (lines 10–11)
steps.body: Line 10: **`q↑.next := p`** ($a_2\to a_1$). Line 11: **`p↑.next := change(t)`** ($a_1\to$ the swapped remainder). `t` was saved on line 9 before line 10 overwrote `q↑.next`.

scene.caption: Result for n = 5: a2 a1 a4 a3 a5

pitfalls: Writing `change := t` on line 8 — the new head must be $a_2$.
Overwriting `q↑.next` before saving `t` — the rest of the list would be lost (the given line order avoids this).

cse-1997-a-53-a.approach: There are $n^2$ vertices, so a spanning tree has $n^2-1$ edges. Every edge weighs $1$ (horizontal or vertical) or $\sqrt2$ (diagonal). The unit edges alone connect the grid, so the MST uses only weight-1 edges.

steps.title: Edge weights
steps.body: Adjacent points differ by at most 1 in each coordinate: horizontal and vertical edges weigh $1$, diagonal edges weigh $\sqrt2$.

steps.title: Lower bound and construction
steps.body: Any spanning tree has $n^2-1$ edges, each of weight $\ge1$, so its weight is $\ge n^2-1$. A "comb" of unit edges (each row joined horizontally, plus the first column joined vertically) is a spanning tree with exactly $n^2-1$ unit edges.

pitfalls: Counting $n^2$ edges instead of $n^2-1$.

cse-1997-a-53-b.approach: Use as many $\sqrt2$ (diagonal) edges as possible. A diagonal step keeps the parity of $x+y$, so diagonal edges form two classes (the two checkerboard colours). A tree on each class uses $n^2-2$ diagonals, and one unit edge joins the two.

steps.title: Diagonals keep the colour
steps.body: A diagonal step changes both $x$ and $y$ by $\pm1$, so $x+y$ keeps its parity. Diagonal edges never join an "even" point to an "odd" one. So a spanning tree contains at most $n^2-2$ diagonals and at least one unit edge between the two classes.

steps.title: Both classes are diagonal-connected
steps.body: For $n\ge2$, each colour class is connected by diagonal moves (for $n=2$: $(1,1)-(2,2)$ and $(1,2)-(2,1)$; larger boards work the same way). So each class has a spanning tree of diagonals: $(\#\text{even}-1)+(\#\text{odd}-1)=n^2-2$ edges.

steps.title: Join and total
steps.body:
One unit edge joins the two trees, giving $n^2-1$ edges in all:
$$w_{\max}=(n^2-2)\sqrt2+1$$

pitfalls: Answering $(n^2-1)\sqrt2$ — diagonal edges alone cannot join the two colour classes.

cse-1997-a-54-a-i.approach: Trace the recursion. With call by value $z$ stays 10 on the way down; the assignments $z:=x+10$ run on the way back, innermost first, so the outermost frame writes last.

steps.title: Going down (z stays 10)
steps.body:
With call by value each call has its own $x$. $z$ changes only on the way back, so on the way down every call adds $z=10$:

| call | $x$ on entry | $x\le40$? | $x:=x+z$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | yes | 20 |
| 2 | 20 | yes | 30 |
| 3 | 30 | yes | 40 |
| 4 | 40 | yes | 50 |
| 5 | 50 | no | — |

steps.title: Coming back (z overwritten)
steps.body:
Each frame sets $z:=x+10$ with its **own** $x$, from the innermost frame outwards:
- call 4: $z=50+10=60$
- call 3: $z=40+10=50$
- call 2: $z=30+10=40$
- call 1: $z=20+10=30$

The outermost call writes last, so $z=30$.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Printed value $= 30$. (`recur` is called 5 times, with arguments 10, 20, 30, 40, 50.)

animation.caption: z := 10, then recur(z)

pitfalls: Taking the innermost assignment ($z=60$) as final — the outer frames write after it.
cse-1997-a-54-a-i.verification: Frame $x$ values after the update are 20, 30, 40, 50; the last assignment made is $20+10=30$.

cse-1997-a-54-a-ii.approach: Count calls in the same call-by-value trace: the argument goes $10\to20\to30\to40\to50$, and the call with 50 fails the test and stops.

steps.title: Arguments of successive calls
steps.body: $z=10$ during the descent, so each call passes $x+10$ to the next: arguments $10, 20, 30, 40, 50$.

steps.title: Stopping call
steps.body: The call with $x=50$ fails $x\le40$ and returns without recursing. Total calls $=5$, counting this last call.

pitfalls: Answering 4 by leaving out the last call, which fails the test but is still a call.
cse-1997-a-54-a-ii.verification: Same table as part (i): calls 1–5, of which the first four recurse.

cse-1997-a-54-b.approach: With call by reference, $x$ is another name for the global $z$, so every update of $x$ changes $z$ immediately. Trace the one shared value.

scene.caption: x aliases z; z doubled to 80

steps.title: Result
steps.body: `writeln(z)` prints $110$.

animation.caption: z := 10, then recur(z)

pitfalls: Forgetting that $x:=x+z$ doubles $z$ when $x$ and $z$ are the same variable.

cse-1997-a-55-a.approach: Count the letters each production adds. With $a$ uses of $S\to bSe$ and $p,q,r$ uses of the recursive rules of $P,Q,R$, the string is $b^{a+p}c^{p+q}d^{q+r}e^{r+a}$. Then eliminate the parameters.

steps.title: Shape of every string
steps.body:
$S\Rightarrow^* b^aSe^a\Rightarrow b^aPQRe^a$, with $P\Rightarrow^* b^pc^p$, $Q\Rightarrow^*c^qd^q$, $R\Rightarrow^*d^re^r$. So
$$i=a+p,\; j=p+q,\; k=q+r,\; m=r+a.$$

steps.title: Eliminate the parameters
steps.body: $i+k=a+p+q+r=j+m$. So every generated string has $i+k=j+m$.

steps.title: Every such string is generated
steps.body: Given $i+k=j+m$, take $a=\max(0,i-j)$, $p=i-a$, $q=j-p$, $r=k-q$. All are $\ge0$, and $r+a=k-j+i=m$. So the condition is also sufficient.

pitfalls: Answering $i=m$ and $j=k$ — that misses strings such as $bccd$ ($i=1,j=2,k=1,m=0$).
cse-1997-a-55-a.verification: $bccd$: $a=0,p=1,q=1,r=0$ derives it, and $1+1=2+0$ ✓. $bbccdd$ ($i=j=k=2$, $m=0$): $4\ne2$, and it cannot be derived.

cse-1997-a-55-b.approach: Two parse trees exist when the same $(i,j,k,m)$ comes from two parameter tuples $(a,p,q,r)$. Find the smallest string for which two values of $a$ are possible.

steps.title: When two trees exist
steps.body: From $p=i-a$, $q=j-i+a$, $r=m-a$, each value of $a$ fixes the whole derivation. Two values of $a$ are possible iff $\max(0,i-j)<\min(i,m)$. This needs $i\ge1$, $m\ge1$ and $j\ge1$ (if $j=0$ then $i-j=i$, so the range is empty).

steps.title: Smallest choice
steps.body: $i=j=m=1$ gives $k=j+m-i=1$: the string $bcde$ (length 4). Shorter strings ($\varepsilon$, $be$, $bc$, $cd$, $de$) have only one possible $a$.

steps.title: The two trees
steps.body:
1. $S\Rightarrow bSe\Rightarrow bPQRe\Rightarrow b\,(cQd)\,e\Rightarrow bcde$ ($a=1$, $q=1$).
2. $S\Rightarrow PQR\Rightarrow (bPc)(\varepsilon)(dRe)\Rightarrow bcde$ ($a=0$, $p=r=1$).

pitfalls: Proposing $be$ — it has only the derivation $S\Rightarrow bSe$ with $PQR\Rightarrow\varepsilon$.
cse-1997-a-55-b.verification: Checked every string of length ≤ 2 in the language: each has exactly one parameter tuple.

cse-1997-b-56-a.approach: Each insertion misses bucket 1 with probability $(n-1)/n$, independently of the others.
cse-1997-b-56-a.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Buckets | $n$, each with probability $1/n$ |
| Insertions | $K$ distinct keys, independent |

steps.title: One insertion
steps.body: $P(\text{key avoids bucket 1}) = 1-\frac1n = \frac{n-1}{n}$.

steps.title: All K insertions
steps.body: $$P = \left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)^K$$

pitfalls: Using $1-K/n$, which treats the events as disjoint.

cse-1997-b-56-b.approach: No collision means all $K$ keys land in distinct buckets (the birthday problem). The $i$-th key must avoid the $i-1$ buckets already used.
cse-1997-b-56-b.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Buckets | $n$, each with probability $1/n$ |
| Insertions | $K$ distinct keys, independent |

steps.title: Key by key
steps.body: Key $i$ avoids the $i-1$ occupied buckets with probability $\frac{n-i+1}{n}$.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body: $$P=\prod_{i=1}^{K}\frac{n-i+1}{n}=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-K+1)}{n^K}=\frac{n!}{(n-K)!\,n^K}$$ For $K>n$ a collision is certain, so $P=0$ (the product contains the factor $0$).

pitfalls: Writing $\binom nK/n^K$ — the order of insertions matters.

cse-1997-b-56-c.approach: The first collision is at insertion $K$ when the first $K-1$ keys go to distinct buckets and the $K$-th key hits one of those $K-1$ occupied buckets.
cse-1997-b-56-c.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Buckets | $n$, each with probability $1/n$ |
| Insertions | $K$ distinct keys, independent |

steps.title: First K−1 distinct
steps.body: Part (b) with $K-1$ keys: $\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-K+2)}{n^{K-1}}$.

steps.title: K-th key collides
steps.body:
Exactly $K-1$ buckets are occupied, so $P(\text{hit}) = \frac{K-1}{n}$. Multiply:
$$P=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-K+2)}{n^{K-1}}\cdot\frac{K-1}{n}$$

pitfalls: Using $1-P(\text{no collision in }K)$ — that is "at least one collision by $K$", not "first collision at $K$".
cse-1997-b-56-c.verification: Equals $P_{\text{none}}(K-1)-P_{\text{none}}(K)$; for $n=2,K=2$: $1-\frac12=\frac12$, and the formula gives $\frac{2}{2}\cdot\frac12=\frac12$ ✓. $K=1$ gives 0 ✓.
